blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — selection of a non-calcium phosphate binder in CKD-MBD
stem: An adult with CKD on dialysis and persistently elevated serum phosphate is prescribed sevelamer instead of increasing a calcium-based phosphate binder. Which rationale is most accurate?

options.A: Sevelamer lowers phosphate by binding it in the gastrointestinal tract without adding a calcium-based binder load, which is useful when calcium-binder exposure is being restricted.
options.B: Sevelamer is preferred because it supplies more elemental calcium than calcium-based phosphate binders while producing a similar gastrointestinal phosphate-binding effect.
options.C: Sevelamer is given intravenously during dialysis and removes circulating phosphate directly from the bloodstream, avoiding the need for gastrointestinal phosphate binding.
options.D: Sevelamer is used mainly as calcium supplementation and has little clinically relevant phosphate-binding activity, so it is selected when serum calcium needs to be increased.

rationale: KDIGO CKD-MBD guidance suggests restricting the dose of calcium-based phosphate binders in adults with CKD G3a-G5D receiving phosphate-lowering treatment. Current sevelamer labeling describes sevelamer carbonate as a nonabsorbed phosphate-binding polymer that binds phosphate in the gastrointestinal tract and decreases intestinal absorption, lowering serum phosphorus. Thus, sevelamer can provide phosphate lowering without adding a calcium-based binder load when limiting calcium exposure is clinically appropriate. Therefore A is correct. B reverses sevelamer's non-calcium property, C assigns an intravenous mechanism it does not have, and D denies its phosphate-binding action.
educational_objective: Recognize why a non-calcium phosphate binder such as sevelamer may be selected when phosphate lowering is needed but additional calcium-based binder exposure is being limited.
